chunks: "I'd say accuracy matters in proportion to the consequence of being wrong, so I look at four things: safety, cost of the battery, how much the user relies on the number, and how hard the load is.

It matters most where an error is dangerous or expensive: drones and aircraft where running out means a crash, EVs where range and a big pack mean every percent is worth real money, medical devices where the battery has to last a guaranteed time, and anything where the warranty depends on usage tracking.
It also matters in grid storage, because usable energy is what you sell.

It matters less in a cheap product where the cell is protected by a hard voltage cutoff and nobody cares if it shuts down a bit early: toys, flashlights, a TV remote, or a small sensor you can swap batteries on.
There a simple voltage threshold is enough. There's also a technical angle: where in the discharge it matters.
The voltage curve is steep near empty, so a voltage threshold is actually fairly good there. In the flat middle it is poor.
And under a heavy pulsed load, voltage-based estimates are the worst, so applications with that profile need the full coulomb counting and model-based approach.
So the answer is to pick the least expensive method whose error still gives an acceptable consequence, and verify it across temperature, load and age."
